en: *Shiji Jigulue Xujì* (Continued Collection of the Brief History of the Shiji), Volume One. Compiled by the monk Dàwén of Qúān at Xiǎngxī in Guī'ān;
edited and published by the layman Qúān, Yán Ěrguī.
It originated with the Great Ancestor, Emperor Chenghiz Khan,
in the second year of the Kaixi era of Emperor Ningzong of the Song dynasty, the year of Bingyin,
when he manifested the Dharma and initiated the destiny of the realm.
He adopted the era name Shengwu and established the state title of the Great Mongol Empire,
with Helin as its capital, known as Shangdu.
In the second year of the Jiaochu era of Zhizhi, the Year of Ji-chou (1249),
Emperor Taizong ascended the throne.
In the sixth year of the Chunyou era, the Year of Bing-wu (1276), Emperor Dingzong ascended the throne.
In the eleventh year of Chunyou, the Xinhai year,
Emperor Xianzong ascended the throne;
this continued until the first year of Kaiping, the Jiwu year.
Qing succeeded to the throne.
In the first year of the Jingding era, the year of Gengshen,
Shizu ascended the throne and proclaimed the Zhongtong era.
Reaching the Jiazi year when the Yuan era was inaugurated,
six reigns spanning fifty-nine years had passed.
Now, the account begins from the first year of the Jiazi cycle of Emperor Shizu.
The successive emperors were Shizu Chengzong, Wuzong, Renzong, Yingzong, Taizong, Mingzong, Wenzong, Ningzong, Shunzong, and Shizu. Shizu’s personal name was Kublai;
he was the uterine younger brother of Emperor Xiaozong.
He ascended the throne in the year Gengshen and extinguished the Song dynasty in the year Jimao.
He inherited the unified empire for sixteen years.
He passed away at the age of eighty. The Emperor was benevolent, sagacious, heroic, and martial, having repeatedly achieved great feats.
He delighted in campaigning against distant barbarians and waged war for many consecutive years.
All submitted to his authority,
and he subsequently unified the realm.
Among his civil officials were figures such as Xu Heng and Yao Shu.
In the imperial court,
military generals such as Buyantu and Dong Wenbing laid out grand strategies that greatly expanded the state’s illustrious achievements in capturing cities and seizing territories.
The establishment of rites and the creation of music brought such abundance and prosperity to the people and all things that it had never been seen before in antiquity. *Yuan Shi* (History of Yuan).
Jiazi, the first year of Zhizheng (*Zhiyuan* in the original text), the fifth year of Jingding of the Great Song. In the seventh month of autumn, a comet appeared in the lunar mansion Liu.
Its light illuminated the heavens, extending for several tens of zhang;
it was seen from the fourth watch in the east and only vanished when the sun rose high. This occurred in the eighth month of that year.
Liu Bingzhong requested that the capital be established in Yan;
the Great Ancestor followed this advice and issued an edict to construct palaces, residences, city walls, and moats.
He designated Yanjing as the Middle Capital (Zhongdu),
changed the era name, issued a general amnesty, convened religious assemblies,
and ordained monks. By imperial decree, he invited the National Preceptor (Guoshi) Bandi Matiye to perform rituals.
Ascending the throne, he was conferred the Secret Precepts. In the eighth month, he was appointed as State Preceptor (*Taibao*) and Grand Master for Splendid Happiness (*Guanglu Dafu*).
He concurrently served as Director of the Bureau of the Imperial Secretariat (*Zhongshu Sheng*). The imperial decree stated:
A Decree from the Emperor, Son of Heaven of Eternal Life: We address you, Liu Bingzhong.
Your spirit is firm and upright, and your learning is profound and refined.
Although you have concealed your traces within the gates of the Empty Gate (Buddhism), [your virtues remain manifest].
Whenever I have applied myself with deep concentration to the Holy Way,
you, Sire, were truly among my attendants while I resided in the Prince’s residence;
it has been more than twenty years since I first heard of your noble character.
You have come from a distant land several tens of thousands of li away.
Now that I have succeeded to the throne,
I require your counsel for the security of the state.
Without first rectifying the titles,
how can one suppress the multitude?
It is fitting that the status of the Master be exalted and that he concurrently preside over the administrative machinery.
He shall be specially granted the rank of Guanglu Dafu Taibao and appointed as Director-General of the Secretariat. You,
sir, must exert yourself in assisting my person.
The Prefect shall first inspect the diligence or indolence of morning and evening duties and deliberate upon the right or wrong of various discussions;
all matters of administration shall be subject to his adjudication and decision.

"Behold his achievements with due distinction; let the imperial insignia be conferred accordingly. This was promulgated throughout the empire. Buyantu was appointed as the Left Chancellor of the Secretariat (Zhongshu Zuochengxiang).
Buyantu was dignified and spoke sparingly; when matters were reported to him by the various ministries...
When there were difficult cases to adjudicate, Buyantu would resolve them with just one or two words.
The officials in the Secretariat were struck with awe and submission, regarding him as a true minister of state. (From the *Yuanshi*)

Yichou (the second year of Zhizheng), the second year of the Zhiyuan era; the first year of the Xiachun era of the Great Song. Last year, in the tenth month, Emperor Lizong passed away, and Emperor Duzong ascended the throne.
His deeds are recorded in the aforementioned work and are not detailed here.
In the first month of spring, on the first day of the lunar month, there was a solar eclipse. In the fifth month, Liu Bingzhong took charge of affairs in the Secretariat;
upon entering for his audience, he took it upon himself to govern the world.
There was nothing he knew that he would not do.
The Shizu consulted him on the great principles for governing the world and the excellent methods for nourishing the people.
Upholding loyalty, he compiled and presented the ancestral statutes and old codes.
He consulted these with what was appropriate in ancient regulations for the present age.
The Emperor praised this,
and on the day the edict was issued, the major principles were established and the minor details unfolded.
At that time, all men of talent were recruited and employed;

culture and civilization flourished, appearing entirely renewed. According to the *History of Yuan*, Xu Heng was summoned to the capital, where he was ordered by the Emperor to deliberate on affairs with the Secretariat (Zhongshu Sheng).
At that time, the Chancellor An Tong was twenty-one years old; having long heard of Heng’s reputation, he admired him deeply.

When he saw him at his temporary residence, he returned home filled with admiration and daily consulted him on matters of state administration. According to the *Yuan Shi*, when Emperor Shizu heard of Zhang Dehui’s reputation, he summoned him for an audience and appointed him as a Councilor of State Affairs in the Secretariat.
He illuminated the profound mysteries of the virtue and conduct of the sages and worthies,
the methods for cultivating the self and governing the state,
and the causes of order and chaos throughout antiquity and the present.
He presented these matters in detail to the Emperor,
who established them as schools for the instruction of the youth;
thus, both the internal and external systems were resplendently renewed.
In the Bingyin year, the third year of Zhizheng (1276), corresponding to the second year of the Xianchun era of the Song dynasty,
one thousand two hundred years had passed since Buddhism first spread to China.
Dingmao, the fourth year of Zhizheng (1297), the third year of the Xianchun era of the Song dynasty: The Song Emperor visited the Imperial Academy to pay homage to Confucius.
He performed the ritual of offering vegetables (*shecai*) and enshrined Yan Hui, Zeng Shen, Kong Ji, and Meng Ke as sacrificial associates.
Sheng elevated Zhuan Sun Shi to the rank of one of the Ten Sages; Xu Heng presented five matters concerning state affairs:
first, the scale for establishing the state;
second, the essential functions of the Secretariat.
Third, he said that it is difficult for a ruler to fulfill his words once spoken.
Fourth, he spoke of agriculture, sericulture, and schools.
Fifth, he advised being cautious regarding minor matters. The Emperor praised these points and accepted them with favor.
He requested to return to his native village, and the Master granted him leave.
This was Chan Master Fuguo; his name was Zhiwen, and his courtesy name was Qiyu.
His posthumous title was Quan-yi,
and his imperial eulogy was Fo-guo Pu-an.
He was the son of the Hao family of Xingzhou.
He attended the tonsure ceremony for Master An of Bianan.
He assisted Master Fu of Wuhuan at Wanshou Monastery and served as an attendant to Master Wansong.
Shortly thereafter, the Grand Guardian (Taibao) Lord Liu was recognized and favored by the Emperor Shizu.
He recommended the Master, who was summoned for an audience; the Emperor was greatly pleased and intended to grant him an official post, but the Master declined, saying:
"The circulation of the Buddha-dharma throughout the world is the wish of this humble monk; wealth and status are not what I hope for.
Emperor Xianzong then appointed Haiyun to preside over the Buddhist teachings.
An imperial edict was issued to the empire to convene a "Fund for Military Supplies" assembly;
the Master upheld this mandate, proclaiming it throughout both the inner court and the outer realm,
and assisted in its successful completion.
Lord Liu, acting under the authority of the Protectorate, conferred this title upon the Master and charged him with the general supervision of the affairs of monks and nuns across all regions.
The Master was resolute in his determination to protect the Teachings.
The monastic community relied upon him.
Later, he submitted his seal and resigned from office on the eleventh day of the fifth month of that year.
He passed away at the Heavenly Palace in Huanzhou due to illness,
passing into nirvana reclining on his right side facing west;
even during the height of summer, his countenance remained as if alive.
Furthermore, there was an extraordinary fragrance.
When his heart, mouth, and teeth were cremated, they did not decay;
even after digging several feet into the ground, śarīras were still obtained.
His age at death was fifty-one;
his years since ordination were forty.
The epitaph was composed by the scholar Yu Ji and is recorded in the Tongzai.
Wuchen, the fifth year of Zhizheng (1268); the fourth year of Xianchun of the Song dynasty. The Yuan generals A-shu and Liu Zheng besieged Xiangyang.
When the Prefect Lü Wenxuan appealed for emergency aid, Xie Fangde’s commentary states:
As an official serving as a Chancellor,
one may grant life or death, and appoint or dismiss others; as an official serving on the Censorate or the Remonstrance Bureau, one [may exercise similar authority].
It can be used to censure and refute those who bring honor or shame upon others;
it serves as the National University (Guozijian) for examining, selecting, and enrolling individuals.
These three ranks are called the "Register of Holy Sages" (shengxian).
In the year Jisi, the sixth year of the Zhiyuan era [1270], the fifth year of the Xianchun era of the Song dynasty [1269], in the second month, the Imperial Preceptor Phagspa...
The Mongolian script was established and promulgated throughout the realm.

In the seventh year of Zhizheng (the *jiwu* year), the seventh year of the Yuan era (*zhìyuán*), corresponding to the sixth year of the *Xiǎndūn* era of the Song dynasty, an imperial edict was issued to invite the Vajrācārya Master Dampa. In Changzhou of the Song dynasty, a rooster grew spurs on its wings. *Gengwu*, the seventh year of the *Zhìyuán* era of the Yuan; the sixth year of the *Xiǎndūn* era of the Song. An edict was issued requesting the presence of the Vajra Master Dampa.
The Abbot of Renwang Temple, the monk Pudu,
and the Imperial Preceptor Bhikṣu Phags pa expounded the ritual manual for the ordination ceremony according to the Mūlasarvāstivāda school.
The Imperial Preface states:
To examine the auspicious fortune of Jambudvīpa,
it has reached the time when the bequeathed teachings of the fourth Buddha, Śākyamuni Tathāgata, are manifest for the benefit of all.
During the reign of the Great Yuan,
the fifth sovereign, Emperor Xuantian Shudao Renwen Yiwu Daguang Xiaoxiao, ascended the throne.
By nature endowed with merit and wisdom, he held firm faith in the Inner Vehicle.
He caused all the myriad states to universally submit to a single transformation;
though the empire under heaven enjoyed boundless peace through his effortless governance,
he looked with favor upon China to propagate the Way.
Yet, he applied himself with tireless diligence,
desiring to personally uphold the Buddha’s lineage and ensure that the succession of masters and disciples continued without interruption; thus,
the correct precepts and ritual protocols have remained unaltered until the present day.
To follow those who practice virtue, one must constantly maintain each [precept] and refine the three karmas while firmly upholding the four modes of deportment.
This is truly the sagacious intent of the Sage Emperor for rectifying the Buddha-dharma, as recorded throughout the annals. Lian Xichan served in court with upright integrity.
The Shizu ordered him to receive the precepts from the Imperial Preceptor Sanghabhadra (Bhikṣu Si-ba-sma).
Xian replied, "I, your servant,
have already received the precepts of Confucius."
The Emperor said,
"Does your Confucius also have precepts?
He replied:
"To be a minister one must be loyal; to be a son one must be filial.
This is correct.

On the eighth day of the twelfth month of the eighth year of Zhizhi (the *xinwei* year), corresponding to the seventh year of the Xianchun era of the Song dynasty, the Great Yuan was first established as its national name.
Adopting the meaning of the "Qianyuan" (Great Origin) hexagram of the *I Ching*,
he first established Mongolian schools at the request of the Grand Guardian Liu Bingzhong, appointing Xu衡 as the Master of Learning.
Heng often said: "If one perceives doubt where there is none in the text, it is because one has not yet mastered it;
when one perceives it as having doubt, one can truly master it.
Only when one perceives no doubt is one truly making progress."
In teaching people, Heng necessarily follows what they already understand and opens up what they have been obscured from seeing.
One should embrace all that is wholesome during its movement and stillness,
relaxing and tightening as required; one must be cautious of its initial sprouts and establish preventive measures through gradual and monthly cultivation.
One does not perceive its transformation for oneself;
as the moon waxes day by day, one does not perceive its change for oneself.
Furthermore, this is the case for the student.
Managing one's livelihood is the foremost priority.
Furthermore, it is said that a scholar-gentleman should take agriculture and sericulture as his means of subsistence.
Ren-shen, the ninth year of Zhizheng (1342); the eighth year of Xianchun of the Song dynasty. Ye Mengding, Imperial Preceptor of the Song, retired to Qin.
He wished that [the Emperor] would exert diligent effort, minimize desires, win the hearts of the people, and consolidate the foundation of the state.
It is further said:
"The matter of integrity and shame is great;
the matter of life and death is small."
He returned directly in a small boat.
Chan Master Pan Gu’s style name was Lishui;
he was a native of Haiyan.
The Master’s appearance was unremarkable,
yet his aspirations were transcendent; he had read extensively through the classics and histories and by nature delighted in the pleasures of mountains and waters.
During the Zhizong era of the Yuan dynasty, he traveled to Mount Wutai, Mount Emei, Mount Funiu, Mount Shaoshi, and other renowned mountains and sacred sites.
He once remarked,
"Half of the world has been covered by my footsteps."
His poetic fame filled the world.
At that time, the Prince of Shen of Goryeo, who was a son-in-law to the Emperor,
heard of the Master’s virtue and reputation and sent a formal letter of invitation.
He lectured on the Great Meaning of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra at Huìyīn Temple in Hangzhou.
The Master deployed his fourfold unimpeded eloquence,
and the seven assemblies were all humbled and won over.
The King was greatly pleased,
and his reputation grew even more esteemed.
Later, he went to a monastery in Song County, where he diligently cultivated the practice of Pure Land.
He recited the name of Amitābha Buddha as his daily practice.
When he was over seventy years old,
he announced his passing in advance without illness, at the appointed time.
He sat upright and entered stillness.
There exists a three-fascicle collection of his mountain-roving poems,
which circulates in the world, as well as the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*.
Guiyou, the tenth year of Zhizheng (the ninth year of the Xianchun era of the Song dynasty). The Yuan had besieged Xiangyang for a long time;
in the second month, they captured Fancheng.
The Commander-in-Chief Fan Tianshun sighed and said:
"Born as a minister of Song, I shall become a ghost of Song upon death.
He then committed suicide by hanging himself at the place where he had been stationed. Xu Heng returned to Huai and Meng.
He severed all social ties and resided constantly at the foot of the mountain,
diligently applying himself to self-cultivation.
The Duke’s love was all-encompassing; though he was not severe, there was order.
Within his inner chambers, it was as if at court, yet husband and wife treated one another like guests.
Mourning rites and sacrifices were strictly observed according to ancient regulations.
This was recorded in the *Huaimeng Huazhi*.
In the year Jiayu, the eleventh year of the Zhiyuan era (the tenth year of the Xiunchun era of the Song dynasty), in the seventh month, Emperor Duzong of the Song passed away.
The Crown Prince, the Young Emperor, succeeded to the throne at the age of four.
In the eighth month, there was heavy rain and flooding, and Tianmu Mountain collapsed;
the waters surged forth, drowning countless people. In the eighth month of that same year, Lord Liu passed away.
He was posthumously granted the title of *Yitong Sanchi Taifu* with the posthumous title *Wenzhen*.
The imperial edict stated:
"A minister serves his sovereign through loyalty and filiality, and it is his noble duty to offer the sincerity of counsel and remonstrance."
The sovereign treats his ministers with propriety and righteousness, contemplating how to deepen the affection between them from beginning to end,
regarding the day of death as no different from the years of life.
Thus, Liu Bingzhong, Grand Master for Splendid Happiness and Grand Preceptor,
had studied to such an extent that he fathomed the ways of Heaven and Man, and his insight penetrated both the present and the ancient.
He was profound and humble, yet possessed firm integrity.
Tranquil and free from ostentation,
you formerly attended the Prince in his private domain and were long accustomed to hearing your lofty discourses;
it was precisely at the moment of the "three audiences" that this occurred.
I have respectfully submitted this ten-thousand-word treatise,
intending to bring the entire world to a state of peace and security,
thereby warning rulers against excessive killing.
I have begun my service as the successor to the throne, and you,
Your Excellency, have exerted your full efforts for the greater part of it.
Indeed, I find that you truly accord with my own heart.
I am fully aware of your intentions;
all matters have been verified,
and you sought nothing else.
For thirty years he served with unwavering dedication, never shirking from hardships;
his hundreds of petitions were incisive and each struck the core of the matter.
Together we shall accomplish the affairs of state;
we were just beginning to plan for the employment of our veteran officials when, alas,
the Compassionate Heaven did not spare even one aged minister.
When I bring this to mind,
how could I ever forget it?
I repeatedly reflect upon your exalted status as a high minister.
Since there was the splendor of the imperial seal of the spring-gate,
he was accordingly granted an edict by imperial decree,
elevating him to the exalted rank of the first grade.
He was thus invested with the *gǔn* robe and ascended to the central position among the three *huái* trees; furthermore,
he was bestowed with a posthumous title to fully honor his extraordinary meritorious service.
May your illustrious spirit recognize my sorrowful favor.
You may be posthumously granted the title of Grand Tutor (Taifu) with the posthumous name Wenzheng (Wen-chen).
[Recorded in] Tongzai: Duke Wenzheng Liu, whose given name was Bingzhong.
His courtesy name was Zhonghuì.
A native of Jiucun in Ruizhou,
he received the tonsure and became a monk under Chan Master Xuzhao of Tianning Temple.
Later, he traveled to Yunzhong and resided at Nantang Temple.
Together with Chan Master Haiyun, he journeyed north to have an audience with Emperor Shizu at his private residence.
At their first meeting, his responses were in accord with the Emperor’s wishes.
From then on, he frequently received the Emperor's inquiries and submitted a memorial presenting several dozen proposals regarding what was appropriate for the current affairs of state.
His ten thousand or so words were all, for the most part, concerned with honoring the sovereign and protecting the people.
The Emperor praised and accepted his counsel;
whenever the Emperor went on military expeditions, he skillfully provided protection and relief.
He saved a great many lives.
Upon ascending to the supreme position of the imperial throne,
he first established court protocol and instituted the system of official ranks.
Regarding the change of the reign era and the establishment of the imperial title, as well as all other matters requiring implementation,
the appropriateness of the times and circumstances were entirely drafted and finalized by the Duke.
The Duke dwelt in seclusion and maintained a vegetarian diet,
remaining serene throughout the day. On the *renxu* day of the eighth month of that year,
he passed away while sitting upright at the age of fifty-nine.
From his youth he was fond of learning, and it did not diminish even unto old age.
Although his rank reached the pinnacle of ministerial office, he remained no different than in his former days.
The Emperor said to his attendants:
Bingzhong has served me for thirty years with a humble mind and prudent secrecy;
his mastery of the arts of yin and yang and the calculation of numbers is profound.
The divination revealed the future as if matching two halves of a tally. The Emperor then commanded Shi Tianze and Bayan to lead an army on a southern campaign,
summoning them to address them with these words:
"In antiquity, the only one who was skilled at taking the South of the River was Cao Bin alone.
If you can refrain from killing, you are my Cao Bin. Shi Tianze was a native of Zhending.
He was eight chi tall with a voice like a great bell.
He was skilled in horsemanship and archery.
He served as a general or a minister for fifty years.
He served as a pillar of state through four reigns and was a model for all officials;
as a founding minister of the nation,
people compared him to Guo Ziyi and Cao Bin.
He was seventy-four years old at death.
His posthumous title was Zhongwu (Loyal and Martial).

*Yihai*, the twelfth year of Zhizheng (*Zhiyuan*) of the Yuan dynasty; the first year of Deyou of the Song dynasty. Emperor Gongzong of the Song changed the era name to Deyou and reigned for two years.
The Yuan troops captured him and escorted him northward; he passed away in the desert. Wen Tianxiang, the Censor-in-Chief of Jiangxi, raised an army to serve the King.
A friend tried to dissuade him, but Tianxiang said:
For more than three hundred years, the state has nurtured its ministers and subjects;
yet when an emergency suddenly arose and troops were summoned from all under heaven,
not a single man nor a single horse came to our aid.
It is because I harbor a deep resentment for this that I,
disregarding my own capacity, wish to sacrifice my life in its service,
hoping thereby to inspire the loyal ministers and righteous scholars of the world.
There will be those who rise up upon hearing the wind of this teaching;
where the principle prevails, strategy is established;
where the people are numerous, strength is achieved.
In this way, the state and its altars may be preserved.
Tianxiang’s nature had been luxurious and his self-indulgence was very great;
at this point, he severely restrained himself and reduced his expenditures.
He exhausted his family’s entire wealth to provide for military expenses.
Whenever he spoke with his colleagues about current affairs,
he would strike the table and weep, saying:
"He who shares in another's joys shares in that person's sorrows;
he who eats another's food must perform that person's duties.
Upon hearing this, there was none who was not moved to emotion. Li Fu, the Judicial Intendant of Hunan, dispatched troops to provide military assistance.
He dispatched three thousand brave warriors and appointed him as their general.
After he had served the King with diligence, he was posthumously honored with the title Zhongjie (Loyal and Integrous).
Hao Jing, an envoy to the Song court, remained detained there for sixteen years.
He compiled various writings and passed away while returning to Yan;
he was posthumously granted the title Wenzhong. Emperor Song issued an edict appointing Zhang Shijie as the General-in-Chief of all the armies.
Later, together with Lu Xiufu and Chen Yizhong, he sailed across the sea to confront the national crisis and perished by drowning. Two stars were fighting in the midst of the sky;
one star fell. On the first day of the sixth month, the sun was eclipsed.
Since then, it has been as dark by day as by night.

On the *bingzi* day of the fifth month in the second year of Shideyou of the Song dynasty—the thirteenth year of Zhiyuan—Song Duanzong ascended the throne and changed the era name to Jingyan. Thereafter...
The mariner Bong arrived at Gangzhou in Lingnan.
On the second month, a black spot appeared in the sun,
as large as a chicken egg.
After they had struggled against one another for a long time, Prime Minister Wen Tianxiang often said, "If the nation perishes, I perish with it; this is the heart of a man.
When the Yuan people led Tianxiang northward, the tides of the Qiantang River failed to arrive for three days.
At that time, the Yuan army was stationed on the banks of the Jiang and Sha rivers;
the people of Hangzhou were just beginning to feel fortunate about this, yet the tides did not arrive. In the third month, the Yuan general Bayan—
Upon entering Lin’an, he raised the great general’s banners and drums.
He received audiences with the Song Emperor, the Empress Dowager, and the various officials, proceeding to the capital to pay his respects. Yao Shu was benevolent, forbearing, and respectful.
He never suspected that others would deceive him;
whenever he consulted with anyone, he always offered sincere advice.
Consequently, there was no one who did not revere him.
At that time, he was appointed as a Hanlin Academician.
All the imperial attendants and scholars of the Song dynasty who arrived at the capital were ordered to follow Xuanzhui in their studies and conduct, after which they were granted official posts.
Dingchou, the fourteenth year of the Zhiyuan era; the second year of the Jingyan era of the Song dynasty.

The Song Emperor was enfeoffed as the Duke of Yingguo and ordered to proceed to the Desima region to study Sanskrit and Tibetan Buddhist scriptures. Empress Quan entered the monastic order at Zhengzhi Temple.
He built the Great Sage Wan’an Temple. Lián Xīxiàn rose to the rank of Chancellor (Pingchang).
Bǎiyán said of him, "Among ministers, he is a true minister; among men, he is a true man."
This became known as his posthumous name.
He passed away at this time.
Wuyin (the 15th year of Zhizhi, the 1st year of Xiangxing of the Song): Emperor Bing of the Song was enthroned and changed the era name to Xiangxing.
Two years after ascending the throne, he sailed by sea to Yashan.
There, Zhang Shijie was defeated in battle by the Yuan forces;
Lu Xiufu took him in his arms and sank into the sea on the first day of the first month.
A great assembly was extensively convened to provide alms for the monastic community, and a general amnesty was proclaimed throughout the realm.
The five elders, including Yuquan, were graced with the imperial favor of ordination. A great star appeared.
It fell into the South Sea,
followed by more than a thousand minor stars;
the sound was like thunder.
It ceased after several hours.
On the day of Jīmòu (己卯), the sixteenth year of the Yuánzhōnɡ (至元) era, in the second month, the Song dynasty perished.
From Emperor Tàizǔ’s rise to power until Emperor Bìng (昺), such was the history of the Song.
A total of three hundred and twenty years.
Wen Mingshan was a native of Gusu;
his courtesy name was Tianxiang.
He was the Imperial Scholar of Song and served as Chancellor, enfeoffed as the Duke of Xingguo.
Possessing the great principles of loyalty and filial piety,
he was captured while witnessing the fall of Yashan.
There was a poem of lamentation which is not recorded here, and another song says:
"The typhoon rises and the sea waters fly; alas!
The civil and military are exhausted, and the Fire Virtue (Hode) is faint. Alas!
Hawks and falcons strike one another; alas, there is nowhere to take refuge! Alas!
The wild geese and white egrets wish to soar; where shall they find a place to return? Alas!
Rowing and singing amidst the midstream, let us go wherever fate leads us! Alas!
"Alone I embrace the Spring and Autumn Annals, yet none understand me—alas! Furthermore, the Song of Righteous Spirit says:
"In heaven and earth there is a righteous spirit;
it is bestowed upon all things in manifold ways to form their shapes."
The conclusion says:
Looking back, that [light] remains bright;
gazing upward, the floating clouds are white.
Long and weary is my heart’s sorrow;
O Heaven, when will it have an end?
The man of wisdom has departed day by day.
The statutes of the law were established long ago.
At the wind-swept eaves, I unroll the book to read.
The ancient Way illuminates my countenance. —Poem on Lingding Bay.
Through hardship and fortune, one scroll of scripture was produced;
amidst falling weapons, four cycles of stars have passed.
Mountains and rivers crumble like waterborne tufts of cotton.
My life adrift like a water chestnut tossed by the wind;
at Kuang-hung Beach, I speak of my fears;
in Ling-ding Bay, I sigh over my loneliness.
In the course of human life, since ancient times, who has not died?
Let me preserve my loyal heart to shine upon the annals of history. Passing through the thatched cottages and deserted palaces of Jinling, the evening glow fades;
like a solitary cloud drifting on, where shall I find reliance?
The scenery of mountains and rivers remains unchanged as before;
The city walls and the people are for the most part no more.

No temple or posthumous title was established. In the ninth month, Wénzōng ascended the throne and changed the era name to the first year of Tiānlì.
In accordance with ritual, Gogebubun was appointed as State Preceptor (Guogong).
The Office for the General Administration of Propagation of the Teachings (Guangjiao Zongguanfu) was established to govern and oversee the monastic community.
Mingzong, whose name was Huashentan, was the eldest son of Emperor Wuzong.
Initially invested as Prince of Zhou,
he went out to serve as a regional commander in Yunnan.
Upon the death of Emperor Taiding,
Emperor Wenzong dispatched envoys to welcome the Emperor [Toghon Temür],
who was then installed on the throne north of He’ning.
Wenzong was established as the Crown Prince;
before long, he died a sudden death, having reigned for barely half a year. Zhang Yanghao had possessed integrity and righteousness from childhood and applied himself diligently to his studies.
He served as Grand Councilor (Zhongcheng) and once authored a work in three volumes.
First is "Loyal Counsel for the Court";
second is "Loyal Counsel for the Censors";
third is "Loyal Counsel for Governing the People."
He passed away at this time.
He was posthumously granted the title of Chancellor (Pingchang) and conferred the honorary epithet Wenzhong.
Wenzong, whose personal name was Tugh Temür,
was the second son of Emperor Wuzong and the younger brother of Emperor Ming.
Originally enfeoffed as the Prince of Huai and residing in Jiankang,
he ascended the imperial throne in the ninth month of the first year of the Zhihe era.
He changed the era name to Tianli, which lasted for two years.
He welcomed Mingzong from the desert sands.
When Mingzong passed away, he ascended the throne.
This was the second year of the Tianli era, the Jisi year.
He established Longxiang Jiqing Temple in Jiankang; he established Chongxi Wanshou Temple on Mount Jiang;

he commanded the officials of the Quanzhang Academy to compile the *Jingshidadian* (Great Compendium for Governing the World); he renamed Jiankang as Jiqing Prefecture; and he appointed the Western monk Ruanzhenkelasi as Imperial Preceptor.
When the Master arrived at the capital, he commanded the court officials from the first rank downward to all welcome him at the outskirts;
when the high ministers prostrated themselves and presented cups of wine, the Master did not move.
Then Bo Mulu'er, the Director of the National Academy (Guozijiao), rose with his cup and stepped forward, saying:
"The Imperial Preceptor is a follower of Śākyamuni and the teacher of all monks under heaven."
I am a follower of Confucius and a teacher of scholars throughout the world;
let us each dispense with formalities.
The Imperial Preceptor rose with a smile,
raised his cup, and finished the drink;
the assembly was struck with awe.
In the first year of the Zhunshun era,
on the gengwu day, Confucius’s father, Shuliang He,
was posthumously enfeoffed as King Qisheng.
His mother was Lady Yan;
she was the Lady Who Illuminated the Sage.
Yanzi was the Duke Who Restored the Sage.
Zengzi was enfeoffed as the Duke of Zongsheng;
Zisi as the Duke of Shusheng;
and Mencius as the Duke of Yasheng.
Huiguang (Shi Rongzhao). His courtesy name was Huiguang.
He received his formal instruction from Huazang and practiced the teachings and contemplations of the Tiantai school.
Later, he followed the Master Yan Zhan, known as Yansou,
at Yanqing Monastery in Huating;
there he applied himself with vigor to the teachings of the Mahāyāna and diligently practiced meditative concentration.
He burned oil lamps to continue his studies by lamplight, never ceasing from morning until evening;
thus, through his resolve, he attained mastery.
He manifested his excellence within the monastic assembly and rose to the rank of Chief Administrator (Zhongyou) for over forty years.
His fame spread throughout the capital, where the Emperor praised him and bestowed a title upon him.
Every New Year’s Day, the Master led the assembly in performing the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* repentance ritual.
To pray for the longevity of the Sage’s life,
beyond the preaching of the Dharma, he performed prostrations and repentance,
sweeping away the dust and obscurations for all sentient beings.
He gathered in roots of goodness;
as he grew old, he became even more diligent.
There were three people who attained his Dharma.
The *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (Sengzhuan) records those named Ju Jian,
Zong Ju, and Zong Quan.
All were dragon-elephants among the Dharma gates. Fan Guo,
courtesy name Deji.
A native of Qingjiang,
he was exceptionally gifted by nature;
though emaciated and living in austere simplicity, he remained pure.
If he could not even bear the weight of his own clothes,
he stood out prominently, setting himself apart from worldly convention;
Wu Cheng recorded this, regarding him as a man of exceptional integrity and solitary conduct.
He may be compared to the gentlemen of the Eastern Han;
this is certainly no empty praise.
The second year of Zhishun, the Xinwei year.
Wu Cheng, Hanlin Academician, passed away.
He authored the *Cuanyan* (Collected Explanations) on the *Yi*, *Chunqiu*, and *Liji*,
as well as edited and collated works such as the *Huangji jingshi shu* and the *Daidai li*.
Enfeoffed as the Duke of Linchuan.
Posthumously titled Wenzheng (Wen- Zheng).
Ren-shen, the third year of Zhishun.
In the fourth month, there was an earthquake on the day of Tian-ning.
In the fifth month, the capital experienced an earthquake accompanied by sounds;
white halos appeared alongside the sun, stretching across the entire sky.
In the eighth month, celestial drums resounded in the northeast; an earthquake struck Longxi in the capital region; and the Emperor passed away at the Upper Capital.
The name of Emperor Ningzong was Yilin Zhenban.
Mingzong was the second son [of Xuanzong].
He was initially enfeoffed as the Prince of Fu.
Upon the death of Emperor Wen, he received a testamentary mandate to succeed to the throne.
The Emperor was seven years old when he ascended the throne;
he passed away after two months in office.
The Great Virtuous One presiding at the altar was named Huìwén.
His surname was Zhang,
and he was a native of Guide.
He left the household life under the venerable monk Gang and received full ordination at the age of twenty.
He received the Bodhisattva precepts from the Venerable Master Wen and succeeded the Dharma-abbot En as the presiding master of the ordination platform. Subsequently,
his religious practice flourished day by day.
His reputation grew increasingly prominent,
and his followers increased in number.
The Master was already strictly observant of the fast and precepts.
He guarded his robes with the utmost care;
even while traveling on the road or staying overnight, his three robes and one alms bowl were always kept by his side.
Day and night he was diligent and earnest, contemplating only the Buddha.
Monastics and laypeople alike followed one another to seek the precepts;
they appeared on the roads in endless succession.
Upon receiving even a single word of instruction, there was none who did not rejoice in their hearts and feel profound gratitude.
He preached the Dharma for over several decades.
He ascended the dharma-seat to bestow the precepts on more than forty occasions.
The high ministers received him with the etiquette due to a teacher.
Those who were transformed by him numbered in the tens of thousands.
On the twenty-second day of the eleventh month of that year,
he passed away at the age of seventy-three, according to the *Fozu Tongzai*.
Shunzong, whose name was Tuohan Temür,
was the eldest son of Mingzong.
During the reign of Wenzong, he was slandered and sent to reside in Guangxi.
When Emperor Ningzong passed away, he ascended the Great Treasure Throne (the imperial throne). He reigned for thirty-six years.
It was during his reign that the troops of the Great Ming entered the capital city.
He traveled to Yingchangfu.
One year later, he passed away.
On the sixth month of the first year of Yuansheng, the Guiyou year.
He ascended the throne on the eighth day of the first month.
He changed the reign title three times:
from Yuantong (2) to Zhiyuan (6), and finally to Zhizheng (27). During these years, Gongxuerjian Zangban Zangbu was formally invited to serve as the Imperial Preceptor.
The Dharma Master from India was named Zhenjing (True Purity);
his courtesy name was Ru’an. He was a native of Huating and a son of the Yao clan.
Her mother, Lady Zhu, dreamed that the moon fell into her lap and she became pregnant.
At the time of his birth, auspicious light filled the room,
and a strange monk appeared.
The Master pointed to his mother and said,
"This child is the reincarnation of the Dharma Master Haiyue.
At the age of nine, he followed Master Mingjing Zhi to study the Lotus Sūtra.
Having committed everything to memory upon hearing it once,
at the age of sixteen he received ordination and exhaustively investigated all the various vehicles (yānas).
He then paid his respects to Master Yunmeng Ze and Master Wujie Du.
He mastered all their teachings.
During the Dade era, he resided at Dezang Monastery in Haiyan;
during the Zhizhi era, he moved to Chaoguo Monastery in Songjiang.
During the Taiding era, he resided at Xiazhu.
He cleared the path in front of the temple, enlarged its gate,
and inscribed "Mount Fuguo" (Buddha-land Mountain) upon it to serve as a sign.
During the Zhishun era, Master Tanzhang Cheng of Upper Tianzhu proposed him as his successor.
He devoted his heart to propagating the Dharma,
and the assembly of followers exceeded a thousand.
The Emperor, admiring his Way,
bestowed upon him the title "Buddha-mind Great Eloquence" (Fuxin Hongbian) as well as robes of purple *kāṣāya* with golden patterns.
The Master recited the *Lotus Sūtra* without ceasing, regardless of cold or heat.
In this year, he manifested illness;
he wrote a verse and passed away.
He was seventy-two years old [in secular age] and fifty-six years of ordination seniority.
At his cremation, his tongue and the bone of his crown remained unburnt.
The relics were five-colored.
The stupa was enshrined at the original mountain monastery.
On the first day of the New Year in the second year of Yuantong, the Jiashu year (1331).
In Bianliang, it rained blood;
those who wore it were all dyed red.
In the third month, in Zhangde, it rained hair-like filaments that were green.
A folk song says:
"When Heaven rains thread,
the people give rise to resentment."

In the lands of the Central Plains, affairs will inevitably change; floods and droughts will occur in rapid succession. In the seventh month, a shooting star like a cup shall appear, red in color and radiant.
In the eighth month, an earthquake shall strike the capital.
At dawn, Mount Ji collapsed,
sinking into a pond a hundred li in circumference.
On the day of Yi-hai, the year was changed to the first year of the Zhiyuan era.

In the second year, the Bingzi year, the earth quaked and mountains split open in Susong; mountains collapsed in Qinzhou; locusts swarmed in Huangzhou; and from spring until the eighth month, no rain fell in Jiangzhe.
The people suffered a great famine, and he provided relief for them.
On the day Dingchou, the fourth month of the third year of Zhizheng (1346),
a comet appeared in the constellation Wangliang.
In the seventh month, he perished within the Guansuo (Girdle) constellation. Regarding the naming and deliberation of the constellations: the Star of Fang governs horses;
it is also called Tian-si (Celestial Chariot).
Because Wang Liang was skilled at identifying horses, it was named after him. In the fifth month, a false rumor spread among the common people.
The imperial court recruited boys and girls;
those available for marriage were nearly exhausted at once. A comet appeared in the northeast. In the seventh month, locusts swarmed in Wushai County.
Yin Zhangkuan looked up to heaven and prayed, saying,
"May it be that I, Yin, be killed rather than the common people be harmed.
Thereupon, black hawks pecked at the locusts.
The entire work titled *Lun Meng Kao Zheng* (Examination and Verification of the Analects and Mencius) composed by Jin Liang was carved for publication.
His disciple Xu Qian wrote the preface.
Xu Qian’s courtesy name was Yizhi.
A native of Dongyang,
he studied under Jin Lixiang, who told him:
In the learning of our Confucian school, the principle is one while the manifestations are distinct.
One need not worry that the principle is not one;
what is difficult is precisely the distinction of the manifestations.
Qian thereby brought about a discernment of the distinctions between social ranks,
while insisting that their ultimate convergence lies in the unity of principle.
He further stated:
The Way of the Sage consists simply in the Mean.
By means of this, the humble person seeks the Mean in every matter and employs it;
he says of himself, "I am not one who possesses great qualities surpassing others."
It is simply that the work of learning must be practiced without interruption.
Its teaching takes the five human relationships as its foundation,
and prioritizes the illumination of the mind and the transformation of one's temperament.
He considered this to be the essential core for establishing one's mind,
and the discernment between what is righteous and what is beneficial to be the standard for managing affairs.
He once said:
Furthermore, there were those who already knew [of this], and they caused others to know it as well.
How joyful this was!
He passed away that year.
He was sixty-eight years old at his death.
His disciples styled him Master Baiyun (White Cloud).

Among his writings were the *Sishu congshuo* (Collected Explanations of the Four Books), the *Shimingwu chao* (Draft on the Names and Objects of Poetry), the *Dushu zhuan* (Traditions for Reading Books), and the *Guanshi* (Observations on History).
He was later posthumously titled Wenyi.
At that time, Chen Luo of Huining and Hu Yigui of Wuyuan were both highly esteemed for their elucidation of Daoxue (Scholarly Learning).
Taibai (Venus) is the image of a High Duke and a Great General.
When it emerges in the east, it should remain subdued in the east;
when it emerges in the west, it should remain subdued in the west.
"Passing noon is called crossing the sky," meaning it is seen above during the day. Venus,
the star of the minor Yin, takes the hours of Ji and Wei as its boundary.
The passage through the heavens as a non-ministerial [sign] portends the rising of military forces.
On the *wùyǐn* day, the first month of the fourth year of Zhìyuán (1267), an amnesty was granted to all under heaven due to an earthquake. In the fourth month, hail fell as large as fists.

In the fourth month of the summer in the fifth year of the Zhizhi era (1268), corresponding to the Jǐmǎo year, there appeared forms such as rings, jade pendants, lions, and elephants. In Xìnzhōu, mountains shook; in Shàowǔ, rain fell to a depth of two *zhàng*;
and in Gǒngchāng, mountains collapsed, burying and killing people.

The filial daughter Cao E was posthumously enfeoffed as Lady Huiganling Xiaozhaoshun Chunyi. In the sixth month, the waters in Tingzhou rose more than three zhang, submerging dwellings and destroying fields;
Venus repeatedly traversed the heavens.
Dharma Master Zongzhou, whose posthumous name was Ziwen and courtesy name Zongzhou,
was a native of Siming.
He received the Dharma from Master Wen of Beixi and emerged as the abbot of Baoyun Temple;
his mastery of both teaching and contemplation was profound and extensive, and his adherence to monastic discipline was extremely rigorous.
In ordinary conversation with others, he was reticent;
yet when ascending the seat to lecture,
he flowed like water pouring down a steep roof.
Nothing could restrain him.
At the time of his death, he lectured on the *Sūtra of the Sixteen Contemplations*.
Upon finishing, he intended to take his seat, part from the assembly, and enter nirvana.
Someone asked,
"The Master has not yet entrusted his final affairs;
how can you suddenly pass into extinction?"
The Master said,
"In the monastic life, one should act as one intends to act.
Do not employ the stratagems of a worldly person, making plans for children and grandchildren and thereby creating complications for later generations."
"Zhòng" (衆) is pronounced with the *yì* (益) rhyme. Thereupon,
he descended from his seat and returned to the abbot’s quarters, where he recorded each item one by one in writing.
He immediately joined his palms and recited the names of the four holy ones of the Western Quarter.
Having completed his dedication of merit and aspirations, he passed away in stillness.
During the cremation, countless relics were produced, as recorded by the monks.
In the gengchen year, the sixth year of Zhizheng (1340), the retired scholar Wu Lai argued that composing literary works is like employing troops:
there is both the regular and the extraordinary.
The "regular" refers to formal rules and regulations.
It is like military formations being clearly distinguished.
That which is extraordinary is not bound by formal laws;
though undergoing a thousand transformations and ten thousand changes, it has never been disordered from the beginning.
Chan Master Tianru, whose name was Weize and whose style name was Tianru,
received the Dharma from National Teacher Zhongfeng.
He resided at Shizi Lin (Lion Forest) in Gusu. His works,

including the *Commentary on the Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, the *Recorded Sayings of the Chan School*, the *Questions and Answers on the Pure Land*, and the *Illustrations and Explanations of the Ten Dharma Realms*,
have been circulated in the world.
Dharma Master Yuancui was a native of Xiaoxi.
He authored works such as the *Collected Annotations on the Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment*,
which remain in circulation today.
Master Xiugeng, whose courtesy name was Yi,
was one of the "Three High Monks" of Yunmen.
He had a collection of poetry and prose.
In the first year of the Zhizheng era, the cyclical year being Xin-si (1341),
the Emperor was viewing the paintings of Emperor Huizong of the Song dynasty and praised them as excellent.
The Academician [Name] stepped forward and said:
Emperor Huizong was capable in many things, yet there was one thing he could not do.
That his person was disgraced and his state destroyed was entirely due to his inability to fulfill the duties of a sovereign.
A ruler values the ability to serve as a sovereign.
Chan Master Yuansou, whose name was Xingduan and whose style name was Yuansou.
He was a member of the He clan of Linhai who entered the monastic life at Huacheng Monastery.
Having attained the essential meaning under Zang-sou of Mount Jing,
in the Gengzi year of the Dade era, he took up residence at Zifú Monastery in Hú.
His fame spread throughout the capital,
and by special imperial decree he was granted the title "Wise and Upright Discernment" (Huìwén Zhèngbiàn).
This was [attested] by Chancellor Zhang Lü.
He moved from Central India to reside at Lingyin Monastery.
An imperial decree was issued to hold a Water and Land (Shuilu) feast at Jinshan Mountain, and the Master was commanded to preach the Dharma;
he subsequently entered the capital for an audience with the Emperor.
His responses to imperial inquiries were so pleasing that he was granted the title "The Sun of the Buddha Universally Shining.
He then returned south to retire in the Western Hermitage.
In the year of Renxu during the Zhizhi era, the assembly requested that he fill the position at Jingshan.
He received three imperial edicts and golden brocade robes, which others considered a great honor;
yet the Master remained as composed as ever.
Previously, when Emperor Duzong of the Song dynasty was performing a *zhao* ritual at the Qin Zhang Hall, he encountered the Supreme Lord (*Shangdi*),
who appointed him to serve as the forty-eighth abbot of Mount Jingshan.
This followed the forty-fourth abbot, Huyan.
"Is the preservation of the Dharma such a trivial matter?
It is all predetermined by the Celestial Court.
When the Master heard this, he was deeply displeased in his heart.
Furthermore, it says that when the Master was in his proper place [in the lineage]:
Chan Master Yuan’an, whose posthumous name was Chaozhi and whose courtesy name was Yizhong.
He was a native of Gusu.
He received the Dharma from Master Yuansou Duan and successively resided at the two monasteries of Longjiao and Puci.
The Emperor bestowed upon him the title Chan Master Mingbian Zhengzong Guanghui.
Subsequently, he ascended to Jingci Temple and then took charge of Mount Jing.
Four times he occupied the high seat to expound the Dharma.
This was done to awaken the ears of humans, devas, dragons, and ghosts.
Monastics and laypeople followed him like clouds gathering toward mountain peaks.
His disciples have compiled the records of his teachings from four assemblies.
Song Wenxuan composed a preface for it,
praising it to the utmost to inspire reverence and faith in others.
The Chan Master Meiwu, whose name was Nianchang.
His family had long resided in Huating.
His surname was Huang.
His mother, Lady Yang, prayed to Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva; she dreamed of an old monk with a bushy beard who sought lodging, and thereafter she conceived.
At the time of his birth, divine light illuminated his room and a rare fragrance pervaded the air.
He entered the monastic life at Yuanming Monastery in Pingjiang,
where he extensively studied a multitude of texts and attended upon Master Xiji Huiji.
He visited Mount Wutai to pay his respects and traveled to Yanjing,
where he was honored by the Imperial Preceptor (Imperial Preceptor of the Yuan) and included among those whose names were inscribed upon the golden-edited Tripitaka.
He then compiled the *Fozu tongzai* (Comprehensive Record of the Buddhas and Patriarchs) in twenty-two fascicles,
which exhaustively documents the historical deeds of the Dharma gate throughout successive dynasties;
its abbot was the monk Zhangbanma of Xiangfu Temple.
Master Yongming, whose posthumous name was Yanshou,
was a native of Siming.
There exists a collection of his writings in circulation. Chan Master Duangiang,
whose name was En,
was one of the "Three High Monks" of Yunmen.
In the second year of Zhèngdé (Renwu), people in Dàtóng resorted to cannibalism; earthquakes were like thunder, and Mount Luófú in Huìzhōu collapsed.
In the third year (Guīwèi), an imperial edict was issued.
He compiled the three dynastic histories of the Liao, Jin, and Song.

Tugh Temür served as the Grand Director of Revision. The Academician Ge Xisi (style name Manshuo), a native of Fengcheng, was consulted by Tugh Temür regarding what should take precedence in governance.
It is said that the priority is to store up talent.
It is appropriate to nurture them while their reputation and standing have not yet flourished,
and to employ them after they have mastered the myriad details of affairs.
He was posthumously enfeoffed as a Duke of Jun with the posthumous title Wen’an.
Dharma Master Zhantang, whose name was Xingcheng:
His courtesy name was Zhantang;
his style was Yuexi.
He was the son of the Sun family of Kuaiji.
Her mother, Lady Jiang, dreamed of the solar disc when she was born.
She received the tonsure and full ordination from Vinaya Master Zhui at Shimen Temple.
She attained a profound mastery of the principles of restraint and maintenance, as well as transgression and violation.
Relying on the Buddha’s discernment, he studied the Tiantai teachings and contemplations under Master Xian;
later, upon meeting Master Yunmeng Ze, he was held in high esteem and deeply honored.
He petitioned the throne to restore the lecture title of Guoqing Monastery in Tiantai.
He traveled to Goryeo to seek the lost writings of Tiantai.
During a severe drought in the regions of Wu and Yue,
the Master led the assembly and preached the Dharma.
He prayed for rain during a year of famine when the people were dying and lacked the means to provide coffins for burial;
he then interred their remains and performed a great Water and Land Assembly to universally deliver them.
During the Zhizhi era, he was summoned by imperial decree to the capital.
He sought instruction in the Way at Myeonginjeon Hall;
by imperial decree, he resided at Cheongtasa Temple.
He was commissioned to revise the Tripitaka and was specially granted a gold-patterned robe.
He was conferred the title of Great Master Fohai.
Later, he returned to Yunwai Zhai in India and then went back to Foguo in Yue,
where he devoted himself earnestly to the Pure Land.
After practicing the threefold contemplation with single-minded concentration for seven days and nights,
he repeatedly experienced auspicious omens.
One day, the Master addressed the assembly, saying:
Today it exists; tomorrow it may not.
How can one toy with the passage of time?
At dawn on the following day, he sat upright and passed away.
He was seventy-eight years of age and sixty-four years since his ordination.
The reliquary remained for seven days, and his countenance appeared as if he were alive.

Among his writings are the *Commentary on the Diamond Sūtra*, the *Annotated Outline of the Heart Sūtra*, the *Commentary on the Disaster-Dispelling Sūtra*, the *Phrase-by-Phrase Explanation of the Amitābha Sūtra*, the *Outline of the Benevolent Kings Sūtra*, and the *Outline of the Cintāmaṇicakra Dhāraṇī Sūtra*.
This continued concurrently with the *Sengzhuan* (Biographies of Monks).
In the fourth year of the Jia-shen cycle, the Zhi-zheng era (1344), the abbots of various mountains requested the restoration of the Office of Monks (*sengsi*), saying: [text continues]
"Being oppressed by the prefectures and counties is like sitting in hell," [the monk] said. Duode replied,
"If you were to establish a monastic office [to oversee them], would that not be like placing one hell within another hell?"
Not permitted.
Dharma Master Xiaoyin, whose name was Xun,
was posthumously titled the Great Chan Master Guangzhi Quanwu.
Emperor Wenzong, out of regard for their former ties from the days when he was still the "hidden dragon," established the Longxiang Dajiqing Monastery and summoned the Master to serve as its abbot.
He was conferred the rank of Grand Master of Central and Great Virtue (Dazhong Dafu) and appointed to oversee the affairs of the monastery.
By imperial decree, he was charged with revising the *Baizhang Qinggui* as recompiled by Dehui.
On the twenty-fourth day of the fifth month of this year, he demonstrated his entry into nirvana.
On the eighth month, he was buried at Balunsan Mountain to the south of the city, adjacent to the stupa of Kang Senghui.
His deeds and traces of the Way [are recorded as follows].
This is fully recorded in Yu Wenzheng’s *Xuegu lu* (Records of Studying Antiquity),
as well as in the stele inscriptions for the two masters Huang Wenchuan and Song Wenchuan.
His dharma-heir disciple was Zongle.
His courtesy name was Jitan.
During the Hongwu era, he served as the abbot of Tianjie Monastery;
his reputation and influence were widely renowned. Thus it is said.
At that time, the Minister of Works was summoned.
Tai You said, "A recluse has no requests of the court;
it is the court that has requests of a recluse."
Why be so stingy with titles and ranks?
In the fifth year of the Zhizheng era, the year of Yiyou (1345), the Imperial Censor [Name] displayed brilliant insight when encountering matters; he would lift his beard in spirited debate.
Whenever celestial portents or calamities befell the people occurred,
he would invariably urge the Emperor to rectify his person and practice cultivation.
"Perhaps the will of Heaven may yet be turned.
His calligraphy was excellent;
after his death, even a single scrap of paper that remained was vied for by people as a treasure.
When the three dynastic histories of Song, Jin, and Liao were completed,
the Emperor said:
"Since the histories have now been compiled as books..."
"Of those who came before me, I shall take their virtues as my model and their failings as my warning.
How much more so for those who serve as rulers and those who serve as ministers!"
One should likewise understand this and take the good and evil of previous generations as a model for exertion.

On the Bingxu day, the sixth year of Zhizheng (1347), there was an earthquake in Shandong that lasted seven days; in Shaowu, there was an earthquake with sounds like the beating of drums; the Yellow River breached its banks; and Li Wei requested that sacrifices be offered at the Altars of Heaven and Ancestors.
"Draw near to upright men and distance yourself from sycophants and the depraved;
thereby honor the Yang and suppress the Yin.
On the first day of the year in the seventh year of Zhizheng, the *dinghai* year.
A solar eclipse occurred during a great cold snap and wind; court officials fell prostrate on the ground. An earthquake struck Dongping;
an earthquake in Shandong destroyed city walls and towers, with a sound like thunder, and the Yellow River shook violently.
Dharma Master Zhuyuan: His name was Shuisheng,
his courtesy name was Zhuyuan,
and he styled himself Wuzhuweng (The Elder Without Dwelling).
He was a native of Leping.
His surname was Fan,
and his mother was Xu.
At the time of his birth, auspicious light illuminated the room.
He received ordination from Master Chang of Mount Yiluo and visited Master Zhong of Yueting.
Seeing a solitary boat crossing the river, he was confident that he could certainly realize the Dharma.
He then made a vow, saying:
"If I cannot become a Buddha in this life, [I shall not cease my efforts]."
When he was about to enter the Avīci Hell,
he experienced moments of awakening through this power several times.
Master Jigong recorded this, saying:
"From this day forward, you shall greatly propagate my school.
During the Tenryū era, the Master was invited to serve as the abbot of Myōkaku-ji Temple on West Lake.
At that time, the high officials maintained a very close relationship with the Master as informal friends.

his temple name was Gwangjong,

On the first day of the ninth month, the Emperor passed away at the Qianqing Palace. On the sixth day of the ninth month, he ascended the throne.
Emperor Shizong Zhehuangdi was the eldest son of Emperor Guangzong.
He was born to Consort Cai;
at the age of fifteen,
upon the demise of Emperor Guangzong, he ascended the imperial throne.

His lifespan was twenty-two years.

The Emperor who Attained Heaven, Proclaimed the Way, Encouraged Filial Piety, and Strengthened Friendship; Honored in Literature, Magnanimous in Arms, Prudent, Tranquil,
Reverent, Dignified, and Wise— his temple name was Xizong,
and he was entombed at De Ling.
In the second month of the first year of the Tianqi era (the Xin-you year),
an "ear" appeared beside the sun, shaped like the moon,
which suddenly resembled a jade ring.
Its magnitude reached to the heavens; for twelve months,
whenever the sun rose, there would suddenly appear an object as large as the sun itself.
Subduing and pressing down upon the sun,
he grinds and washes it away. Master Zhanran resided at Yunmen and transmitted the Caodong school.
He founded Xinggu Monastery and constructed a sea embankment.

The final verse says:
"For more than forty years, I have not dwelled upon my achievement."
Exhausting one’s resources again and again, they turn into no trace;
now, having exhausted them until there is nowhere to rely,
one finally realizes that all previous efforts were applied in error.
He passed away on the twentieth day of the seventh month in the seventh year of the Tianqi era.
